lines.note: Zuga completes Miz-zuga from f468: water remains or is held. The preceding page's zuga is therefore a catchword, not another occurrence in the body; a agoa has a visible word division here.

runs.text: que não ſe entorne, ou corra, &c. ¶

lines.note: The water neither spills nor runs out. A new example begins Ta-, the opening of tamaranu, whose negative form is used emphatically below.

runs.text: maranu yoi, l, varui fitode gozaru.

lines.note: Tamaranu modifies yoi or warui hito, an extraordinarily good or bad person. The Portuguese translation begins Ho-, continuing as homem on the next row.

runs.text: mem tão bom, ou tão ruim queſe não pode ſo-

lines.note: The person is so good or bad that the degree cannot be borne. The printed queſe is retained as a close-set form rather than silently modernized.

runs.text: frer, & aßi ſerue este negatiuo pera encarecer

lines.note: Frer completes sofrer; the explanation explicitly states that the negative is used to intensify an expression, not necessarily to describe literal suffering.
Muito as cousas completes the account of emphatic intensification. This short continuation closes the cross-page tamaru entry.

runs.text: O terſe, ou ſofrer. Mas não ſe vſa ſòſẽ

lines.note: Tamari names enduring or holding out but is said not to be used alone without another word. The initial is T, and the close-set phrase retains its grave and nasal abbreviation.
The usage restriction continues into an example: hitotamari mo koraeji, not being able to endure even briefly. Its final quotation construction continues below.
To zonzuru completes 'I think that ...'; Taif. cites book 16 of the literary source. The citation label is upright, while Lib. 16 and the Portuguese translation are italic.

runs.text: não poderei eſtar, ou deter me nem hum ta-

lines.note: The translation says the speaker cannot stay or hold out even for a very little while. Ta- begins the diminutive tamanino on the next row.
Manino completes the printed diminutive; tamarigatai then gives the sense of being difficult or impossible to endure. The Portuguese negative phrase continues below.

runs.text: ſe tenha, ou não ſe pode ſofrer, &c.

lines.note: The gloss says no one can hold out, or the situation cannot be borne. It closes the endurance entry before the unrelated seasoning sense.

runs.text: Hum licor muito ſaboroſo que ſe tira

lines.note: This tamari is a flavorful liquid obtained from miso. Its culinary sense is separate from the preceding noun for endurance.

runs.text: do Miſò, & ſerue pera temperar o comer.

lines.note: The flavorful liquid is drawn from miso and used to season food. The mark over the final o is retained as the baseline grave in Miſò: the nearby upward curve belongs to long s, not a second circumflex stroke. The Japanese food name is embedded in Portuguese.
Tamarimizu is impounded or retained water. The initial T and the a in repreſada correct the OCR's F and u.
The water is held somewhere, completing the preceding definition. The nasal abbreviation in algũa remains over its printed carrier.
Tamasakana describes something rare or infrequent, directly matched by couſa rara. The printed long s is preserved.
Tamasakani is the corresponding adverb, 'rarely'. The example begins Ta- and continues on the next physical line.
The example describes happening to meet or encounter someone. The caron in mairiyǒte is retained; the Portuguese idiom continues below.
Por marauilha completes the sense of a rare or unexpected encounter. It is the old Portuguese adverbial expression, not simply an exclamation of wonder.
Tamasuri denotes a lapidary, matching Lapidairo. The historical Portuguese spelling is kept rather than replaced by a modern form.

Tamatama and tamatamano denote rarity. The abraded medial t of the headword is supported by the repeated stem and the supplied NINJAL lexical index; the scan's form is retained rather than OCR Tamaama.

runs.text: Boceta rica de que vſão as mo-

lines.note: Tamatebako is an ornate box used by women. The worn headword is read from its surviving types as Tamatebaco, not Famaebaco; mo- continues as molheres.
Lheres completes molheres, the women who use the box. The short line closes the entry without further information about its contents.
Tamatsubaki is marked poetic and equated with tsubaki. The initial T and medial ma are worn but supported by the visible word; the P. is upright.

runs.text: ta aruore que dà hũas fulas vermelhas.

lines.note: The tree bears red flowers or growths. The source's unusual fulas is retained as visible rather than silently replaced with flores or folhas; the earlier OCR tu arure is corrected to ta aruore.
Tamawari is giving by an honored person to another person. Dar, not Dur, begins the Portuguese definition; ou- continues the recipient description.

runs.text: tra ſomenos, ou a peßoa igual. Vt,

lines.note: The recipient may be inferior or equal in rank. Catana- begins the illustrative object, a sword, and is continued with the object particle below.
Catana wo tamawaru means giving someone a sword. The Portuguese repeats Catana as a Japanese item name within its explanatory sentence.
A further written-language use of tamawaru means eating. Na, rather than OCR Ni, introduces the Portuguese register qualification; the cited Japanese verb is roman.
The eating sense is used when speaking of oneself. This pragmatic restriction completes the preceding supplementary meaning.
Tamashii is the soul. Qimo and tamaxijuo begin expressions for astonishment; the Q has a visible tail, correcting OCR Oimo, and the headword has no extra i after Ta.
Kesu completes the expression for being amazed or frightened. Admirarſe is one printed word; the next example begins Ta-, not OCR la-.
Tamashii mi ni sowazu is glossed as the same astonishment, or not being oneself. Idem and the explanatory Latin alternative marker belong to the italic apparatus.
Em si completes 'not being oneself', the Portuguese description of discomposure. It remains an independent physical row of the same example.
Tamaya is a tomb or the building containing one. The initial letter is T rather than OCR F; the close-set daqual is retained.
The building contains a grave, completing the architectural alternative for tamaya. The final vowel of eſtà and the undivided ſepultura correct OCR eſti and ſe paltura.
The next tamaya is a lapidary who works precious stones. The first letter of Lapidairo is L, not I; the Japanese headword likewise begins with T, not F.

runs.text: Tamayura. P. i, Tçuyuno vouoqu aru tei.

lines.note: Tamayura is a poetic expression explained as the condition of abundant dew. The small equivalent marker is i, not OCR l, and the printed vouoqu is preserved without normalizing its vowels.

runs.text: Modo de estar muito orualho junto. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The Portuguese confirms much dew gathered together. Item then introduces a further temporal meaning, completed on the next row.

runs.text: Breue eſpaço de tempo, ou vida.

lines.note: The second sense is a short interval of time or life. It is linked to tamayura, not to the following grass name.
Tamazusuki is a poetic name associated with susuki grass. The initial is T and P. is upright; the source does not print an i marker before Suſuqi.
The grass is tall and grows abundantly. This completes the descriptive botanical gloss without imposing a modern taxonomic identification.
Tamazusa is a poetic word for a letter. A further sense concerns the manner of tying written paper; the upright P. is separate from the italic gloss.

runs.text: de dar nò em algum papel eſcrito como carta

lines.note: The explanation describes knotting a written sheet, such as a letter. The scan reads como carta, not OCR coma carta; the grave in nò is retained.

runs.text: que ſe manda, ou verſos eſcritos, &c.

lines.note: The sheet may be a letter to send or written verses. The conjunction is ou, visibly distinct from the OCR's ampersand.

runs.text: Pera, he propoſição de genitiuo: tambem

lines.note: Tame is glossed as 'for' and described as a genitive-related preposition, with a further use continuing in column 2. The printed-looking propoſição is retained as an apparent spelling anomaly rather than silently modernized to preposição; the OCR's severely garbled line is replaced from the scan.
The final figure is worn; its remaining loop and tail, together with the folio sequence, support 239. rather than the OCR’s 230. This is a chosen reading, not a perfectly preserved digit.
The account of tame continues: it also functions as a noun. The printed close-set nomeſubstantiuo corrects OCR substautiuo; the example begins 'this is for you'.
Mede gozaru completes core wa otame de gozaru. The translation is 'this is for you'; the initial of Isto is I, not OCR E. The line is indented like the continuation above it.
Tame gives forms for holding or restraining something. The following example illustrates not stopping even for a single step.

runs.text: Vareuo mite fitoaximo tameide nigue yu-

lines.note: Ware wo mite hitoashi mo tameide nige yuku describes fleeing on seeing the speaker without pausing. The historical negative tameide is retained, not modernized to a newer inflection.

runs.text: Vendo me não podendo deter ſe nem

lines.note: Qu completes yuku; Fab. is an upright source label. The Portuguese begins the translation about not being able to stop on seeing the speaker.

runs.text: hũ ſô paßo, ſe acolheo. ¶ Item, Endereitar.

lines.note: The person fled without a single step's pause. Paßo corrects OCR vaßo, and the clearly upward mark over o is retained; Item introduces the separate sense of straightening.
Ki wo tame naosu is straightening a piece of wood. The verb begins tame, not OCR came, and the Portuguese describes straightening some piece of wood.
The figurative example concerns correcting someone's bad habit. Fitono restores the worn t, and cuxe is the regular historical spelling of kuse, not an anomalous word.

runs.text: Emendar o ruim custume, ou manha dalguem.

lines.note: The Portuguese confirms reforming someone's bad habit or manner. Custume is supported by the remaining types and its clearer repetition later in the column; the OCR's ou bune is not meaningful text.
Teppoo wo tamuru illustrates aiming a gun. The worn m in tamuru corrects OCR ta nuru; the close-set Japanese phrase remains undivided as printed, and eſ- continues below.
Pingarda completes espingarda, the firearm used in the aiming example. The short continuation remains separate from the next noun.

runs.text: Couſa torta que ſe endireitou: cõmum-

lines.note: Tame now describes something crooked that has been straightened. The following lines explain its usual construction when the former bend returns.

runs.text: mente ſe vſa com este verbo vocoru. Vt,

lines.note: The noun is commonly combined with okoru, occurring here as vocoru within Portuguese explanation. The example begins Ta-; the introductory Vt has a visible comma.
Tame ga okotta means the bend has returned. The Portuguese says the object has become crooked again, continuing through the divided couſa.
The figurative example applies recurrence to the soul, anima no tame ga okoru. Animano, with a worn n, corrects the OCR's Auimano; the Portuguese explanation follows below.

runs.text: Tornarem abrotar os meſmos vicios, ou

lines.note: Ru completes okoru; the same vices are described as springing up again. The entire Portuguese sentence, including its initial T, is italic rather than the OCR's mixed styling.
The recurring faults may also be passions of the soul. This completes the metaphor of an old bend returning after straightening.
Tameire denotes straightening or correcting someone. The gloss divides emendar across this line and the following row.

runs.text: dar faltas, ou vicios dalguem. Vt,

lines.note: Dar completes emendar, correcting someone's faults or vices, not the OCR's dur. Hito wo ta- begins the corresponding Japanese example.
Meiruru completes tameiruru in hito wo tameiruru, to correct a person. The brief continuation is not another headword.
Tamen is equated with nemuru, sleeping, and translated Dormir. The supplied Japanese equivalent is retained without adding an unattested qualifier.
Tamengoromo is everyday clothing, explained as ke no koromo. The unusual printed spacing Q eno is retained as graphic evidence, not interpreted as separate Japanese Q and eno words.

runs.text: do que hum traz de ordinario, ou de còte.

lines.note: The clothing is what someone wears ordinarily or habitually. The historical Portuguese expression de còte and its accent are retained.

The verb means watching or waiting for an opportunity. The initial is T; the last headword type looks r, with a shoulder and no independent i dot, so Tamerar is retained as a possible printed anomaly rather than silently replaced by the Tamerai of the supplied NINJAL lexical index. The subsequent examples clarify the intended verb. Lexical aid: NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, v202510, CC BY 4.0; the supplied scan remains authoritative for transcription.

runs.text: occaſião pera fazer algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The verb includes waiting for an occasion to act. Toogoku begins a literary example involving forces from the eastern provinces.

runs.text: no xei coreuo mite teqica, micatacato ta-

lines.note: The eastern forces see something and consider whether it is enemy or ally. The Japanese hesitation verb is physically divided after ta-.
Merai completes tamerai, followed by wondering or doubting. Taif. is the upright source label, not OCR Faif; the following lowercase lib. and book number are italic.

runs.text: A gẽte dos reinos do Leste estãdo vendo, &

lines.note: The Portuguese identifies people or forces from the eastern provinces who are looking and considering. A is visibly separate from the abbreviated gẽte, correcting OCR Agẽte.

runs.text: duuidando ſe erão inimigos, ou gente de ſua par

lines.note: They doubt whether the people are enemies or on their own side. The physical line ends with par without an established hyphen, and its continuation indentation is restored.
Te completes parte; the next example is considering the world or public opinion. Tamerǒ begins with t, not OCR c, and con- begins the Portuguese considerar.

runs.text: ſiderar o que paßa no mundo, ou como ſe toma

lines.note: The gloss concerns considering what happens in the world and how something may be received. The line ends toma without an added hyphen before the continuation rà.

runs.text: rà algũa couſa da gente, ou ſe ſe notarà, &c.

lines.note: The question is how people will take something, or whether it will attract notice. The repeated ſe belongs to the Portuguese syntax and is not an accidental duplication.
Tameshi is proof, trial, or experience. Tame- begins the phrase tameshi ni hiku, which is explained on the next two rows.

runs.text: Trazer, ou alegar por proua, ou

lines.note: Tameshi ni hiku means adducing something as evidence or precedent. The Portuguese offers both bringing forward proof and invoking old custom.
Custume antiguo completes the old-custom alternative. Both historical spellings and the provisional st expansion are retained rather than normalized.
Tameshi gives forms of tamesu, testing or trying. The principal part eita is a historical inflection and is not replaced with a modern shita ending.
Katana wo tamesu is testing a sword. Catana appears again as a Japanese item name within the Portuguese gloss and is flagged for optional whole-word typeface review.
The historical dictionary illustrates sword testing by cutting a dead body. A separate example begins Fito-, with a worn t rather than OCR r, and concerns testing a person.
Uo tamesu completes hito wo tamesu, trying or testing someone. The Portuguese description continues with its human object below.
Dalguem completes the sense of making a trial of someone. The brief continuation is distinct from the following word for the populace.
Tami is the people or common populace. The Portuguese plebea supplies the social distinction explicitly.
Tamyoo or tameyooji is another name, clarified by bechi no na. The Portuguese explanation concerns a different name adopted by a member of the same family.

runs.text: me, ou alcunha que algum da meſma familia

lines.note: The alternate name may be a name or surname taken within a family. The divided nome is preserved across the two physical rows.

runs.text: toma differente por algum reſpeito, como de

lines.note: A different family name is taken for some reason, with adoption or acknowledgment as the example that follows. The historical reſpeito is preserved.

The name may be that of the person who adopted or acknowledged the bearer as a child. The surviving strokes and this context support quem perfilhou, correcting qtem perſilhou; f is lexical here, not a long-s allograph.
Tamochi gives forms of tamotsu, holding or keeping. The principal part otta is retained as supplied by the source.
Yo wo tamotsu is possessing or governing the realm. Ter corrects OCR Fer; go- continues as uerno on f470, while the separate bottom uerno is the catchword.
The italic catchword continues the preceding go- and repeats the next page opening. Its middle and final letters are faint; uerno is the incorporated reading supported by that continuation.
